- `AskConversationScope`: `#suggested-prompts`.
- `PromptSendingScope`: how a send button's prompt is sent.

#### Card Format

Every question is told how an answer hands back prompts and questions in the forms the [AskConversationScope](../ask-conversation/index.md#ask-conversation-scope) shows as cards, so whenever the user asks for a prompt, it comes back as a card they can send to Code, Chain, or Spec. It is not a project's to edit or leave out: the application adds it to each question's <task-instructions> block, after the project's Ask instructions, on a paragraph of its own, whatever those say, including a project's Ask instructions saved before it was added, which are kept as they are. Its text is baked into the application from this application's own repository, in `ask-cards.md` in its `.suspense/system-prompts` directory beside the defaults, and a build can't be made without it. It is never given to a task, and Freeform sends nothing. It says:
Whenever the user asks you for a prompt, or your answer suggests one for them to send, give each prompt as a fenced code block whose info string is `suspense-prompt` and the mode it is for, one of `code`, `chain`, `spec`, `ask`, or `freeform`, such as ```` ```suspense-prompt chain ````, holding only the prompt's text, ready to send, never as plain text, a quote, or any other code block, since only this form lets the user send it from your answer. Pick the mode that fits the work, `chain` when it changes both the spec and the code; the user can send it to Code, Chain, or Spec all the same. When you need the user to answer something before you can go on, write the question as a fenced code block whose info string is `suspense-question`, the question on its first lines and then, if there are answers to pick from, one per line, each starting with `- `. Use these blocks only for prompts and questions meant for the user, never for code or examples.

#### Saving

Each project has its own system template, instructions, and injected prompts, saved with its data, as the [ProjectDataScope](../../project-data/index.md#project-data-scope) says, a Markdown file each, system.md for the system template, code.md, combined.md for Chain, spec.md, and ask.md for the modes, and edited in the [SettingsWindowScope](../../settings-window/index.md#settings-window-scope). One with no file yet gives its default.

#### Understanding File

Each Code, Chain, or Spec task has an understanding file: the short list of constraints the harness has taken from the spec for it, which the [RightSidebarScope](../../../ui/components/right-sidebar/index.md#right-sidebar-scope) shows as it changes. It is saved beside the task's history record, with the same name and the extension `.understanding.md`, written by the harness itself. Nothing else writes it, and nothing is there until the harness writes it. Each constraint links to the compiled reference file it comes from, never to the spec's source.

#### Defaults

The defaults are the prompts saved in this application's own repository, in its `.suspense/system-prompts` directory, named as a project's are. They are the source of truth for the defaults, and are baked into the application when it is built, so a build always ships with whatever those files say, and changing them changes the defaults the next build has. A build can't be made without them.
The system template's default says what the project is, where its code is and where its spec is, each on a paragraph of its own, so the one a run can't see goes, that each prompt starts with a <task-instructions> block saying what that prompt is for and what it may change, and then SPEC_READING on a paragraph of its own. It holds no fluency.
The spec-reading prompt's default says:
Read the spec from its compiled reference under ${HARNESS_DIRECTORY}/reference, where inheritance, expressions, and links are already resolved, or, for one thing, from what `piton slice` prints for it with this harness's adapter.

Never read the .pi source under ${SPEC_LOCATION} to learn what the spec says; that is only where edits to the spec go.

Before executing anything, read the spec it touches. Links to ${HARNESS_DIRECTORY}/reference/... in the prompt are the spec for what they name. Read each one you need before changing anything it covers. Don't re-read something you've already read.
The Spec and Chain defaults have, after what the mode is for, on a paragraph of its own:
Before creating or editing any .pi file, read ${PITON_FLUENCY_FILE} once in this conversation, unless you already have: it is how Piton is written.
and then, on another:
Open a .pi file only to change it. Once you have changed the spec, run `piton check` and fix every error it reports, then run `piton build` and check the result in the refreshed reference under ${HARNESS_DIRECTORY}/reference, not by reading the source again. Never finish with a spec that `piton check` or `piton build` reports errors in.
The Code, Chain, and Spec defaults then end with, on a paragraph of its own:
Before changing anything, write the constraints this task must meet to ${UNDERSTANDING_FILE}, and keep it current as you read more of the spec. It is a Markdown list and nothing else: one line per constraint, at most twelve, each a single short, specific statement of what must be true, written as a link to the compiled reference file it comes from, such as `- [The chain tab has no bottom border in combined mode](${HARNESS_DIRECTORY}/reference/scope/prompt-mode/chat-input/index.md#chain)`. Only list what the spec says; leave out anything you are deciding yourself. Replace a constraint when you learn it was wrong rather than adding another.
The Code, Chain, Spec, and Ask defaults each have, after what the mode is for, on a paragraph of its own:
When the work is about Suspense, its modes, its prompts, or its questions, or you are to write a prompt or a question for the user, first read ${SUSPENSE_FLUENCY_FILE} once in this conversation, unless you already have: it is how Suspense works.

content.text:
Every question is now told to give prompts as `suspense-prompt` blocks, and each prompt card has Send to Code, Send to Chain and Send to Spec buttons. The last full test run passed (508); two earlier runs each failed a different pair of tests that also passed on their own, and those tests have flaked in earlier tasks. I haven't asked a real question in the app to see a card or click the buttons.

**How questions are told:**
- **The text:** it's in `.suspense/system-prompts/ask-cards.md`, built into the app (`system_prompts::ask_cards()`).
- **Where it goes:** it's added to the end of every question's instructions, after the project's own Ask instructions, whatever they say. That includes a project whose Ask instructions are empty or were saved before this change, so the project you had in mind gets it without resetting anything. Tasks and Freeform never get it.
- **Defaults:** the old card paragraph is gone from the default `ask.md`, so it isn't said twice.
- **Suspense fluency:** `suspense-fluency.md` now says a prompt card has buttons that send it to Code, Chain or Spec.

**Prompt cards** (`src/prompt_mode/ask_pane.rs`):
- **Buttons:** Copy, Edit, then Send to Code, Send to Chain, Send to Spec, each in its mode's colour, 4px apart and wrapping on a narrow card.
- **Highlighting:** the button for the card's own mode is filled in its colour and the others are ghosts. An `ask` or `freeform` card adds a filled "Ask" or "Send to Freeform" first. A card with no known mode shows all three as ghosts.
- **Sending:** clicking one sends the prompt straight away in that mode, as if typed on that tab and sent. A task queues if its lane is busy. It uses the Slice toggle as it is, sends nothing attached, and leaves whatever you're typing alone. For Chain, it also follows your Post-Build Spec Update toggle.
- **After a click:** the button reads "Sent to Code" (and so on) with a check for 2 seconds, and can be clicked again.
- **Edit:** does what "Send to prompt" used to: it puts the text in the chat input on the card's mode tab, or Chain for a card with no mode, and reads "Edited" for 2 seconds.
- **Tooltips:** each send button says what it does, as "Send this prompt as a Code task".

**One choice of mine:** the filled button's text is black on a light mode colour and white on a dark one.

I updated the existing tests for the new card buttons and question instructions, and added a check that a Send button creates the task without touching the chat input. The spec and the prompt agree.

The Gmail, Google Calendar and Google Drive connectors still need authorizing in your claude.ai connector settings, and the `backlog` MCP server didn't start. None of them were needed here.
